_about: Local legend card on region hubs (site/sections/_legend.py). Keys are the region's display name as the page shows it (a state, province or country). Without an entry the legend is picked from the data: most famous cases located in the region, then places and old newspaper reports, then the creature index's sightings count. Living traditions are never auto-picked. Fields: creature (slug, required), blurb (one line, optional), places (extra place slugs to link, optional), case ([path, label], optional).

West Virginia.blurb: Point Pleasant has a Mothman museum, a stainless steel statue downtown and a festival that fills the streets.

United Kingdom.blurb: Loch Ness in Scotland is where the modern lake monster craze took off, after the Mackay sighting in 1933.

British Columbia.blurb: Okanagan Lake's serpent has had its own statue on the Kelowna waterfront since 1960.

New Jersey.blurb: Asbury Park closes Cookman Avenue every year for the Jersey Devil Festival.

New Mexico.blurb: The Roswell debris story from 1947 put New Mexico on the UFO map, and Roswell still throws a festival for it every Fourth of July weekend.

Washington.blurb: Ape Canyon on Mount St. Helens is named for a 1924 story of miners besieged by rock-throwing apemen.

California.blurb: The name took off at Bluff Creek in 1958, and Patterson and Gimlin filmed their figure along the same creek in 1967.

Vermont.blurb: Lake Champlain's long-necked monster, made famous by the Mansi photograph in 1977.

Texas.blurb: Texas is where the goat-sucker turned into hairless dogs, like the Cuero carcass in 2007.

United States.blurb: The best-known cryptid in North America, from Bluff Creek in California to Ape Canyon in Washington.

Canada.blurb: Sasquatch, from the Ruby Creek incident in 1941 to the museum in Harrison Hot Springs, BC.

Ohio.blurb: Ohio's own Bigfoot, named for the flattened grass nests it's said to build, from the 1978 Minerva Monster to Salt Fork State Park.
